unit.title: Designing and governing agents at school

lesson.title: Evaluate before you trust
lesson.subtitle: A test set, an honest score and every failure read

video.title: Evaluate before you trust
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education, Bangladesh (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)

chapters.label: The pass mark, and testing again

scenes.visual: A list: Five questions, all right; Enough to rely on?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Our new agent got my five test questions right. So the whole staff can use it tomorrow, yes? Five questions isn’t a test. It’s a first impression.

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how to evaluate an agent before anyone relies on it.

scenes.visual: A list: Many requests, known answers; Scored the same way; Read every mistake.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Evaluating an agent is like setting an exam. You write many requests whose right answers you know. You score every answer the same way. And you read every mistake, not just the score.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A fair exam mixes seen questions with new ones. For an agent: wordings it was trained on, and new ones people really use. Darsi Tiny is right about ninety-seven percent of the time on trained wordings, about seventy-nine on new ones.

scenes.visual: A list: Fixed requests; Known answers; Kept out of training; Run after every change.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A test set is a fixed list of requests with their right answers, kept out of training. Run it again after every change, and you’ll know whether the agent got better or worse.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the evals lab, Darsi Tiny scores twenty-nine out of thirty-two. That’s sixteen of sixteen on trained wordings, but thirteen of sixteen on new ones. The Arabic new wordings were weakest: six of eight.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our agent scores twenty-nine out of thirty-two. What should we look at next?

scenes.visual: A list: “the term battery”; Wrong words as a name; A library request refused; Guard it, or don’t use it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The three failures. Explain the term battery became a search for the term battery. In Arabic, wrong words were copied as a pupil’s name, and a library request was refused. Each tells you what to guard, or what not to use it for.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Set the pass mark before you test, by the stakes. A helper that looks up library books might pass at ninety percent, with a quick check. Anything that messages parents or touches records needs a person’s yes, whatever the score.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Test again after every change. In the teach lab, Darsi Tiny learned a bus tool from sixteen examples. With no old examples mixed in, it got seven of eight bus requests right, but only one of eight old skills.

scenes.visual: A list: Run all 32; Compare the columns; Read every failure; Test the taught model.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the app, run the whole test of thirty-two requests, and compare the two columns. Read every failure. If you taught Darsi Tiny the bus tool, test that model too.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. After teaching it a new tool, the new tool works. What must you test before you use it?

scenes.visual: Summary points: Many requests, known answers; Score exactly; read failures; Pass mark first; retest.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Many requests, known answers · Score exactly; read failures · Pass mark first; retest
scenes.narration: The new tool and every old skill. Remember: a test set is many requests with known answers. Score it exactly, and read every failure. Set the pass mark first, and test again after every change.

scenes.visual: A list: Pupils write the exam; Five requests, right answers; Both languages, a new wording; Keep the best twenty.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: pupils write the agent’s exam. Each group writes five requests with the right answers, in both languages, including a new wording and one to refuse. Keep the best twenty as your school’s test set.

checkpoints.prompt: Our agent scores 29 out of 32. What should we look at next?

options.text: The three failures, and what they have in common
A bigger model with a higher score

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the failures show where it breaks: new wordings, copied words, a wrong refusal. That tells you what to guard.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a score hides where it fails. Read the three failures first.

checkpoints.prompt: After teaching it a new tool, the new tool works. What must you test before you use it?

options.text: The new tool and every old skill

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — learning something new can make a model forget: with no old examples mixed in, Darsi Tiny kept only 1 of 8 old skills.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a new skill can push out old ones. Test the new tool and every old skill.
